Severe, irreversible hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure have been reported, particularly in patients with Cockayne syndrome. 3. Metronidazole has been shown to be carcinogenic in mice and rats, with tumors affecting the liver, lungs, mammary glands, and lymphatic tissues. It is unknown whether metronidazole is carcinogenic in humans. 4. Hypersensitivity reactions may occur in individuals allergic to bismuth subsalicylate, aspirin, other salicylates, metronidazole, other nitroimidazole derivatives, or tetracycline. 5. Co-administration of metronidazole with methoxyflurane can result in fatal renal toxicity. 6. Tetracycline use during pregnancy can cause fetal harm, including rare but serious maternal hepatotoxicity at high doses (>2 g IV). 7. Tetracycline use during tooth development (last half of pregnancy, infancy, and childhood up to 8 years) may cause permanent tooth discoloration (yellow-gray-brown) and enamel hypoplasia. 8. Known or previously unrecognized candidiasis may become more symptomatic during metronidazole therapy, requiring antifungal treatment. 9. Tetracycline hydrochloride use may lead to overgrowth of nonsusceptible organisms, including fungi. If superinfection occurs, discontinue therapy and initiate appropriate treatment. 10. Photosensitivity reactions, such as exaggerated sunburn, have been observed in patients taking tetracycline. Patients should avoid direct sunlight or UV light exposure and discontinue treatment at the first sign of skin erythema. 11. Bismuth-containing products may cause temporary and harmless darkening of the tongue and/or black stools, which generally resolve within several days after stopping treatment. Stool darkening should not be confused with melena. 12. Metronidazole should be used cautiously in patients with a history of blood dyscrasias, as mild leukopenia has been observed during its administration. Total and differential leukocyte counts are recommended before and after therapy. 13. Severe hepatotoxicity and acute hepatic failure, including fatal cases with rapid onset, have been reported in patients with Cockayne syndrome receiving metronidazole. 14. Prescribing antibiotics in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection increases the risk of drug-resistant bacteria and is unlikely to benefit the patient. 15. Metronidazole may interfere with certain serum chemistry determinations, such as AST, SGOT, ALT, SGPT, LDH, triglycerides, and hexokinase glucose. 16. Bismuth absorbs X-rays and may interfere with gastrointestinal tract diagnostic imaging. 17. Patients with hepatic impairment metabolize metronidazole more slowly, leading to plasma accumulation. Therapy should be used cautiously in mild to moderate hepatic impairment and may not be appropriate for severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C). 18. The use of bismuth subsalicylate/metronidazole/tetracycline is not recommended in children or teenagers recovering from varicella (chickenpox) or influenza due to the risk of Reye syndrome. 19. Tetracyclines may increase BUN levels, and higher serum concentrations can lead to azotemia, hyperphosphatemia, and acidosis in patients with severe renal impairment. 20. Tetracycline use during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy can cause permanent tooth discoloration in infants and potentially inhibit bone development. 21. Administration of oral tetracycline to pregnant rats has resulted in yellow fluorescence in the teeth and bones of newborn animals. 22. Metronidazole use during pregnancy has been associated with certain congenital anomalies. 23. Tetracycline and metronidazole are present in human milk at concentrations similar to maternal serum levels. 24. It is unknown whether bismuth subcitrate is present in human milk or its effects on the breastfed infant or milk production. 25. Tetracycline binds to calcium in human milk, reducing its oral absorption in infants. 26. Metronidazole transfers to human milk, and infant serum levels can approach therapeutic levels. Due to potential tumorigenicity shown in animal studies, breastfeeding women should pump and discard milk during therapy and for 2 days after therapy ends. 27. Metronidazole and tetracycline inhibit nucleic acid synthesis by disrupting DNA. 28. Bismuth subsalicylate has antisecretory effects via salicylate and antimicrobial action via bismuth. 29. Tetracycline inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 30S and possibly 50S ribosomal subunits of susceptible bacteria. 30. Tablets and capsules should be taken at mealtimes and bedtime. Bismuth subsalicylate tablets should be chewed and swallowed, while metronidazole tablets and tetracycline hydrochloride capsules should be swallowed whole with a full glass of water (8 ounces). 31. Adequate fluid intake, especially with the bedtime dose, is recommended to reduce the risk of esophageal irritation and ulceration caused by tetracycline hydrochloride. 32. If a dose is missed, continue the normal dosing schedule without taking double doses. If more than four doses are missed, contact the prescriber. 33. Blister packs should be stored at room temperature (20-25°C [68-77°F]). 34. Adding plans allows for comparison of formulary status with other drugs in the same class. Formulary information may vary and should be confirmed with the applicable plan provider for the most current details. 35. Breastfeeding women should be informed of the potential risks and advised to use stored milk or formula during therapy with metronidazole.
